extracted.intended_audience: math olympiad contestants, coaches, and advanced problem solvers (USAMO/IMO level)
extracted.subtask_description: Worked solutions and solution techniques for high‑school olympiad problems (geometry, combinatorics, number theory, inequalities, polynomials). Presents multiple approaches, lemmas, and common proof strategies used in contest solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of classical number‑theory results (Fermat's Little Theorem / modular arithmetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Fermat's Little Theorem and modular arithmetic to reduce expressions modulo primes and show divisibility (e.g., showing p divides a_n by evaluating powers mod p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check small primes separately (p=2,3 as done). Reduce exponentials modulo p−1 where applicable and simplify to constants (example: 2^{p−1}+3^{p−1}+6^{p−1} ≡ 6 (mod p)). Show the factor that is relatively prime to p to conclude divisibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit equal radii via Extended Law of Sines in geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: When two circumcircles have equal radii (from equal sines of corresponding angles), use the Extended Law of Sines to deduce a common second intersection point and derive equal lengths/isosceles triangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equality of sin values to infer equal circumradii R and then identify the second intersection O of circles; deduce AO = CO etc. This can lead to rotations/spiral similarities mapping vertices and corresponding points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geometric rotations and spiral similarities to map configuration points
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a rotation (or composition of rotation + homothety = spiral similarity) centered at a fixed point to map one vertex to another and infer mappings of other points (e.g., H(A)=C ⇒ H(D)=B and H(F)=E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the appropriate center (intersection of circumcircle perpendicular bisectors or center of spiral similarity) and apply it to deduce equal angles, lengths, cyclic quadrilaterals and common intersection points for families of circumcircles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use directed angles modulo π and relabeling if unfamiliar
rubrics_metrics.description: Angles may be taken directed modulo π (180°) throughout geometric arguments; if the reader is not familiar, relabel vertices to obtain an equivalent configuration without directed angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State explicitly that angles are directed modulo π where used; alternatively reindex vertices (e.g., relabel ABCD as CDAB) to avoid sign/ordering confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify a fixed point common to a family of circumcircles by multiple methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that circumcircles of a parametrized family of triangles all pass through a single fixed point (other than an obvious common point) by providing several independent constructions (center of rotation O, intersection X of perpendicular bisectors, center Y of spiral similarity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present multiple proofs (e.g., equality of radii; perpendicular bisectors; spiral similarity center from intersecting circumcircles) to show robustness; note that these constructions coincide (O = X = Y) and parts of proofs are interchangeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Simson line or known triangle theorems where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize standard configurations such as the Simson line relative to a fixed point and triangle, and apply known consequences (collinearity of feet, cyclic quadrilaterals) to conclude cyclicity of quadrilaterals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show perpendicular feet are collinear and deduce equal subtended angles leading to cyclicity; reference known theorems to shorten arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model combinatorial contest problems as graphs/multigraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate problems about contestants solving problem pairs into a (multi)graph with problems as vertices and edges weighted by number of contestants who solved that pair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use properties of the constructed graph (degrees, parity, modular invariants) to derive contradictions or bounds. E.g., build graph contestant by contestant and track degree changes modulo 3 to exploit invariance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counting / double counting and define appropriate variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce counts p_{ij} (number of contestants solving problems i and j) and n_r (number of contestants solving exactly r problems), sum over pairs or contestants to obtain inequalities relating these quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the same total in two ways (sum over pairs vs sum over contestants). Use given lower bounds on p_{ij} to derive linear inequalities and deduce bounds on n_r (for example showing n_5 ≥ 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use extremal/minimal counterexample strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a counterexample exists with minimal size or minimal number of a certain feature; then modify the instance (add/remove contestants/diagonals) to derive contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After minimality assumption, show additional structure must hold (e.g., all others solve exactly 4 problems) and reach contradiction via counting or construction removal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modular / residue class invariants (mod 3 arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Track degrees or counts modulo a fixed integer (e.g., modulo 3) to exploit invariance under allowed operations and obtain contradictions in parity/residue patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adding contestants contributes fixed increments (e.g., +3 to some vertex degrees), deduce that degrees are invariant modulo that base after initial configuration and compare with target multigraph residues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive counting on combinatorial / triangulation structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove upper bounds on number of special triangles (good triangles) in a triangulation by induction on the number of polygon sides/segments contained inside a diagonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up lemma bounding good triangles on a diagonal that contains n sides; handle base cases n=1,2 then induct using internal point splitting (pick a triangle PiPaPj) and sum bounds for subarcs, decreasing the RHS by 1 when the central triangle is/ is not good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit parity properties and odd/even counts in polygon decompositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize 'good segments' by parity (odd number of sides) and note that isosceles 'good triangles' must have exactly two good sides; use parity to assign disjoint sides to triangles and obtain an upper bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For triangulations, assign to each good triangle a pair of sides that belong to no other good triangle; this injective assignment yields an easy global bound (≤ 1003 in the 2006-gon example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalize homogeneous inequalities (scale or set a+b+c = 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with homogeneous inequalities, fix a convenient normalization (e.g., a+b+c = 1) to reduce variables and simplify minimization problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After scaling, express differences as new variables (e.g., x = a−b, y = b−c) to reduce to a two-variable inequality; exploit homogeneity to search for extrema more easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor cyclic symmetric polynomials to expose key factors
rubrics_metrics.description: For cyclic symmetric homogeneous polynomials, factor out obvious cyclic factors (a−b)(b−c)(c−a)(a+b+c) to get a lower‑degree symmetric factor and simplify inequality analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that P(a,b,c)=ab(a^2−b^2)+... is divisible by (a−b)(b−c)(c−a)(a+b+c); write explicit factorization to reduce the problem to bounding the remaining linear factor under normalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use calculus or inequality methods (AM-GM) to find minima/maxima
rubrics_metrics.description: After reducing to one- or two-variable functions, find extrema by taking derivatives (find critical points) or using AM-GM estimates to bound expressions and identify equality cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check derivative critical points and verify global minima; alternatively use AM-GM to get lower bounds and determine when equality occurs. Compare both methods for robustness (as done for f(x) with x=1/√2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor and gcd reasoning in Diophantine equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor expressions (y−1)(y+1) = 2^something × other factors, analyze gcd constraints and parity to deduce possible factor shapes, and reduce parameter ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit that consecutive integers have small gcd, write factors as powers (2^m etc.) times odd parts, bound odd parts, and test small possibilities (e.g., m odd, m=3 leading to specific solution). Use elementary bounding to exclude ranges and pin down exact solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use substitution and bounding on integer parameters to restrict possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate factorization into exponential Diophantine relations with parameters m,n and bound n (e.g., show 3<n<7 so n=5) by inequalities and growth comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine inequalities derived from factorization with monotonicity/growth rates to force small finite ranges for parameters; then check remaining cases directly to find solutions or contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of integer fixed points of polynomial iterations via degree arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: For P polynomial of degree n>1 with integer coefficients, and Q the k‑fold iterate, show Q(t)=t can hold for at most n integers by relating integer cycles to roots of P(x)+x=c of degree n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the set S_P of integer fixed points of P and S_Q of Q. For t∈S_Q but not S_P, form the cycle t0,t1,...,tk−1 and show any other s0 in S_Q between t0 and t1 leads to s0 being a root of P(x)+x=t0+t1; since P(x)+x has degree n there are at most n such integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define geometric antipoint and use convexity arguments for area bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign to each side of convex polygon a weight (area of largest triangle with that side). Define an 'antipoint' as a farthest polygon point from the side; show antipoint is a vertex whose parallel through it doesn't cross the interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use convexity to argue existence and properties of antipoints; use minimal counterexample and transformations (reduce to polygon with opposite sides parallel, then parallelogram) to show the sum of assigned areas is at least twice the polygon area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use transformations on polygons to reduce complexity (remove parallel‑opposite sides / reduce to parallelogram)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a convex polygon violating a desired inequality, transform it by cutting off or replacing parts to obtain a polygon with fewer nonparallel sides while tracking area and assigned weights to reach contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful area bookkeeping: compare increases/decreases in assigned weights vs area changes; show transformed polygon remains a counterexample contradicting minimality, thereby forcing existence of a parallelogram case which yields equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide multiple independent solutions and cross‑check equality cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, present several different proof methods (synthetic, analytic, combinatorial) for the same statement, and verify equality/extremal cases across methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent approaches (e.g., rotation/spiral similarity, perpendicular bisectors, law of sines) to confirm a fixed point exists; for inequalities, use both calculus and AM-GM to locate same minimizing configuration to validate result.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and prove auxiliary lemmas separately to modularize proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolate frequently used or 'well‑known' facts into lemmas (e.g., M is circumcenter of triangle IBC when M is second intersection of AI with circumcircle) and prove them before using in main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label lemmas clearly, give concise proofs, and then reference them in the main solution to keep the main flow readable and logically modular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle trivial or degenerate cases explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Before nontrivial manipulations, check easy cases (equal variables, small primes, side counts that make LHS zero) and state that if these occur the inequality/statement is trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., in the inequality assume wlog a>b>c because if not LHS=0; in number theory check x=0 or small x separately. This prevents invalid normalizations or divisions by zero.
